turns.response_html:
Building an automated tool to scrape your history from [gemini.google.com/app](https://gemini.google.com/app) requires bypassing Google’s strict authentication and anti-bot mechanics. Instead of writing complex login scripts that fail against 2FA, the most resilient engineering approach for a CLI tool is to use Playwright connected via Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) to an already authenticated, running browser session.

Here is a comprehensive blueprint to build a Python-based CLI tool that executes this exact workflow, handles HTML-to-Markdown conversions to preserve formatting, and enforces your required directory architecture.

Architectural Workflow

  1. Launch Browser in Debug Mode: Open Chrome or Firefox with a dedicated debugging port.
  2. Attach CLI Tool via CDP: Hook Playwright into that open instance to inherit your active Google session.
  3. Crawl Chat Links: Parse the Gemini sidebar navigation list to extract all conversation URLs and titles.
  4. Scrape & Convert sequentially: Step through each URL, locate the conversation container, sequentially isolate user turns from model turns, convert the HTML to clean Markdown text, and save them.

The CLI Tool Implementation

1. Prerequisites & Dependencies

You will need playwright for browser orchestration and markdownify to ensure that code blocks, tables, and bold markdown tags are cleanly preserved when parsing the web UI’s inner HTML.

pip install playwright markdownify
playwright install chromium

2. Python CLI Script (gemini_exporter.py)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import re
import sys
import argparse
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
from markdownify import markdownify as md

def slugify(text):
    """Sanitizes text to safe directory names."""
    text = re.sub(r'(?u)[^-\w.]', '_', text.strip().replace(' ', '_'))
    return text[:50] if text else "untitled_chat"

def parse_and_save_chats(output_dir, port):
    with sync_playwright() as p:
        cdp_url = f"http://localhost:{port}"
        print(f"[*] Connecting to browser session via {cdp_url}...")
        
        try:
            browser = p.chromium.connect_over_cdp(cdp_url)
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"[-] Error: Could not connect to browser. Is it running on port {port} with debugging enabled?")
            sys.exit(1)
            
        context = browser.contexts[0]
        page = context.new_page()
        
        print("[*] Navigating to Gemini dashboard...")
        page.goto("https://gemini.google.com/app")
        page.wait_for_timeout(3000)  # Allow time for dynamic sidebars to fully render
        
        # Pull chat link nodes from sidebar (match elements linking to an explicit app conversation state)
        # Gemini uses dynamic paths containing /app/<id>
        links = page.locator("a[href*='/app/']").all()
        chat_queue = []
        
        for link in links:
            href = link.get_attribute("href")
            title = link.inner_text().split('\n')[0]  # Avoid trailing UI junk
            full_url = f"https://gemini.google.com{href}" if href.startswith('/') else href
            if full_url not in [c['url'] for c in chat_queue]:
                chat_queue.append({"url": full_url, "title": title})
                
        print(f"[+] Discovered {len(chat_queue)} unique chat threads.")
        
        for index, chat in enumerate(chat_queue, start=1):
            print(f"[{index}/{len(chat_queue)}] Processing: {chat['title']}")
            page.goto(chat['url'])
            
            # Allow virtual scroll content and chat streams to settle
            page.wait_for_load_state("networkidle")
            page.wait_for_timeout(2000)
            
            # Create the distinct bottom-up structure
            safe_title = slugify(chat['title'])
            chat_root = os.path.join(output_dir, f"{index:03d}_{safe_title}")
            prompts_dir = os.path.join(chat_root, "prompts")
            responses_dir = os.path.join(chat_root, "responses")
            
            os.makedirs(prompts_dir, exist_ok=True)
            os.makedirs(responses_dir, exist_ok=True)
            
            # Select target blocks containing the sequential conversation stream
            # Gemini abstracts prompt elements inside tags like 'user-query' or '.query-text'
            # Responses are held within 'message-content' tags or '.model-response'
            turns = page.locator("user-query, message-content, .query-text, .model-response").all()
            
            prompt_counter = 1
            response_counter = 1
            
            for turn in turns:
                tag_name = turn.evaluate("node => node.tagName.toLowerCase()")
                class_attr = turn.get_attribute("class") or ""
                
                # Check structural heuristics to distinguish Input vs Output
                is_prompt = "query" in tag_name or "query" in class_attr
                
                # Extract inner HTML so markdownify can maintain code snippets and structural lists
                raw_html = turn.inner_html()
                if not raw_html.strip():
                    continue
                    
                markdown_text = md(raw_html, heading_style="ATX").strip()
                
                if is_prompt:
                    filename = f"{prompt_counter:03d}_prompt.md"
                    with open(os.path.join(prompts_dir, filename), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                        f.write(markdown_text)
                    prompt_counter += 1
                else:
                    filename = f"{response_counter:03d}_response.md"
                    with open(os.path.join(responses_dir, filename), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                        f.write(markdown_text)
                    response_counter += 1

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Gemini Chat History Exporter CLI")
    parser.add_argument("-o", "--output", default="./gemini_history_backup", help="Target output directory")
    parser.add_argument("-p", "--port", type=int, default=9222, help="Remote debugging port for your browser")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    
    parse_and_save_chats(args.output, args.port)

How to Execute the Script

To hook this tool into your browser, you must spin up an instance that exposes a debugging port.

Step 1: Open Your Browser in Debugging Mode

Make sure your browser is completely closed before launching it via your terminal:

For Chrome (macOS):

/Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222

For Firefox (macOS):

/Applications/Firefox.app/Contents/MacOS/firefox --start-debugger-server 9222

(If navigating on Linux or Windows, substitute the path strings to match your binary paths.)

Step 2: Authenticate

In the new browser instance that opens, navigate to [https://gemini.google.com/app](https://gemini.google.com/app) and ensure you are logged into your Google account.

Step 3: Run the Tool

Run your CLI tool from another terminal instance to parse the DOM, split the content, and generate your isolated structures:

Ah, the classic path mismatch. When you pip install playwright, the CLI binary gets tucked away into your Python site-packages or user binaries directory, which Fish doesn't see globally by default.

You can bypass the global command lookup entirely by running the package directly through Python:

python3 -m playwright install chromium

Why this happens (and how to fix it permanently)

If you plan to run playwright commands directly frequently, here is how to handle it based on how you installed it:

  • If you are using a virtual environment (recommended): Make sure you activate it using Fish's explicit activation script before running the tool: 
    source .venv/bin/activate.fish
  • If you installed it globally via pip: Python's user binary path isn't in your environment $PATH. You can append it to your Fish path by running: 
    fish_add_path ~/.local/bin
    (Note: If you're on macOS using an Intel/Apple Silicon global Python setup, the path might be ~/Library/Python/3.X/bin instead).

turns.prompt_text: [*] Connecting to browser session via http://localhost:9222... [-] Error: Could not connect to browser. Is it running on port 9222 with debugging enabled?
turns.response_html:
This is the most common trap with Chrome's Remote Debugging. If you already have Chrome running normally on your machine, launching it from the terminal via /Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/... doesn't actually spin up a new isolated process. Instead, it just opens a new window inside your existing running Chrome instance, completely ignoring the --remote-debugging-port flag.

Because of this, Playwright is knocking on port 9222 and finding nobody home.

Here is how to force Chrome into a true isolated debugging session, even if you have your regular browser open.

The Fix: Force an Isolated Profile

You need to pass a temporary --user-data-dir flag. This tricks Chrome into starting a completely distinct process with its own sandbox, allowing the debugging port to open properly.

Run this from your Fish shell:

# 1. Create a temporary profile directory
mkdir -p /tmp/chrome-debug

# 2. Launch Chrome with both the port and the custom profile
/Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome \
  --remote-debugging-port=9222 \
  --user-data-dir=/tmp/chrome-debug

How to verify it's working

Before running your Python script, you can verify that Chrome is actually listening on that port. Open a second terminal window or split your pane and run:

lsof -i :9222

If it's working, you'll see Google Ch or Chromium listed as LISTEN.

Moving to a fully automated approach is much cleaner. Instead of dealing with separate terminal sessions, profile locking flags, and debugging ports, we can pass browser lifecycle management entirely to the script using a Persistent Context.

The tool below launches its own dedicated browser session using an isolated local directory (./gemini_profile) to keep things self-contained. The very first time you execute it, the script pauses and asks you to log into Google in the window that appears. Once you are authenticated, it intercepts the redirect and completes the download automatically. On every subsequent run, it remembers your login state and runs entirely hands-free.

1. Clean Automated Architecture

Here is the revised Python engine (gemini_backup.py). It uses Playwright's Chromium binary (which runs independently from your system Chrome or Firefox) to ensure web components render identically without touching your personal browser configuration.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import re
import sys
import argparse
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright
from markdownify import markdownify as md

def slugify(text):
    """Sanitizes chat thread titles for the file system."""
    text = re.sub(r'(?u)[^-\w.]', '_', text.strip().replace(' ', '_'))
    return text[:50] if text else "untitled_chat"

def run_backup(output_dir, profile_dir):
    with sync_playwright() as p:
        print(f"[*] Initializing browser with profile cache: {profile_dir}...")
        
        # Creates or targets an isolated local session folder
        context = p.chromium.launch_persistent_context(
            user_data_dir=profile_dir,
            headless=False,  # Headed mode required for initial login / view state stability
            args=["--no-sandbox", "--disable-setuid-sandbox"]
        )
        
        page = context.new_page()
        print("[*] Navigating to Gemini...")
        page.goto("https://gemini.google.com/app")
        
        # Heuristic check to see if the user needs to log in
        page.wait_for_timeout(2000)
        if "accounts.google.com" in page.url or page.locator("a:has-text('Sign in')").count() > 0:
            print("\n" + "="*60)
            print("[!] AUTHENTICATION REQUIRED")
            print("[!] Please complete your Google sign-in within the opened browser window.")
            print("[*] The script will auto-resume the moment you hit the Gemini Dashboard.")
            print("="*60 + "\n")
            
            # Wait indefinitely for the user to log in and get redirected back to the core app
            page.wait_for_url("https://gemini.google.com/app*", timeout=0)
            print("[+] Login detected! Starting text collection sequence...")
            page.wait_for_timeout(3000)

        # Ensure elements are present on the screen
        try:
            page.wait_for_selector("a[href*='/app/']", timeout=15000)
        except Exception:
            print("[-] Error: Chat history sidebar links failed to load. Check authentication.")
            context.close()
            sys.exit(1)
            
        # Extract unique thread URLs from the sidebar
        links = page.locator("a[href*='/app/']").all()
        chat_queue = []
        for link in links:
            href = link.get_attribute("href")
            title = link.inner_text().split('\n')[0]
            full_url = f"https://gemini.google.com{href}" if href.startswith('/') else href
            if full_url not in [c['url'] for c in chat_queue]:
                chat_queue.append({"url": full_url, "title": title})
                
        print(f"[+] Discovered {len(chat_queue)} chat threads.")
        
        # Sequential processing loop
        for index, chat in enumerate(chat_queue, start=1):
            safe_title = slugify(chat['title'])
            print(f"[{index}/{len(chat_queue)}] Processing thread: '{chat['title']}'")
            
            page.goto(chat['url'])
            page.wait_for_load_state("networkidle")
            page.wait_for_timeout(3000)  # Safe delay for content chunks to hydrate
            
            # Generate the distinct hierarchical directory layouts
            chat_root = os.path.join(output_dir, f"{index:03d}_{safe_title}")
            prompts_dir = os.path.join(chat_root, "prompts")
            responses_dir = os.path.join(chat_root, "responses")
            
            os.makedirs(prompts_dir, exist_ok=True)
            os.makedirs(responses_dir, exist_ok=True)
            
            # Compound CSS selector pulls turns in exact chronological sequence order
            turns = page.locator("user-query, message-content, .query-text, .model-response").all()
            
            prompt_counter = 1
            response_counter = 1
            
            for turn in turns:
                tag_name = turn.evaluate("node => node.tagName.toLowerCase()")
                class_attr = turn.get_attribute("class") or ""
                
                is_prompt = "query" in tag_name or "query" in class_attr
                raw_html = turn.inner_html().strip()
                if not raw_html:
                    continue
                
                # Transform rich layouts (lists, code blocks) to Markdown text strings
                markdown_text = md(raw_html, heading_style="ATX").strip()
                
                if is_prompt:
                    filename = f"{prompt_counter:03d}_prompt.md"
                    with open(os.path.join(prompts_dir, filename), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                        f.write(markdown_text)
                    prompt_counter += 1
                else:
                    filename = f"{response_counter:03d}_response.md"
                    with open(os.path.join(responses_dir, filename), "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                        f.write(markdown_text)
                    response_counter += 1
                    
        print(f"\n[+] Extraction complete. Data preserved in: {output_dir}")
        context.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Clean, hands-free Gemini History Markdown Exporter")
    parser.add_argument("-o", "--output", default="./gemini_markdown_history", help="Target output folder")
    parser.add_argument("-c", "--cache", default="./gemini_profile", help="Session persistence profile folder")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    
    run_backup(args.output, args.cache)

turns.response_html:
Google’s authentication gates are incredibly aggressive at spotting automated browsers. Pivoting to a user-driven, high-level extraction strategy is smart.

Trying to control the macOS cursor directly via OS macros (like pyautogui) can get incredibly brittle because web layouts shift, sidebar elements require scrolling, and window sizes change. Instead, the cleanest, most bulletproof hybrid approach is to use the browser’s own JavaScript engine to pull the HTML directly while you are normally logged in, and then let a local Python CLI tool build your folder structure.

This bypasses all bot detection, avoids messing with cursor coordinates, and runs completely within your regular browser profile.

The Workflow Blueprint

  1. The Collector: You paste a lightweight JavaScript snippet into your browser’s DevTools console. It automatically clicks through your Gemini sidebar threads, scrapes the raw HTML conversation turns, and downloads a single data dump file (gemini_dump.json).
  2. The Processor: You pass that single JSON file to a local Python CLI utility, which handles the HTML-to-Markdown translation and automatically generates your strict directory tree.

Step 1: The Browser Console Collector

Open Chrome or Firefox, navigate to [https://gemini.google.com/app](https://gemini.google.com/app), open your DevTools Console (Cmd + Option + I), paste this code, and press Enter:

(async () => {
  const sleep = ms => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms));
  
  // Scrape unique conversation links from the sidebar
  const links = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll("a[href*='/app/']"));
  const uniqueChats = [];
  const seen = new Set();
  
  for (const l of links) {
    const href = l.getAttribute('href');
    if (!seen.has(href)) {
      seen.add(href);
      uniqueChats.push({ href, title: l.innerText.split('\n')[0] });
    }
  }
  
  console.log(`[+] Found ${uniqueChats.length} chats. Starting automated click-through...`);
  const masterDump = [];
  
  for (let i = 0; i < uniqueChats.length; i++) {
    const chat = uniqueChats[i];
    console.log(`[*] Processing [${i + 1}/${uniqueChats.length}]: ${chat.title}`);
    
    const element = document.querySelector(`a[href='${chat.href}']`);
    if (element) {
      element.click();
      await sleep(3500); // Safe hydration delay for long chat structures
      
      // Isolate prompts vs responses using target DOM elements
      const turns = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll("user-query, message-content, .query-text, .model-response"));
      const parsedTurns = turns.map(t => {
        const tag = t.tagName.toLowerCase();
        const cls = t.getAttribute('class') || '';
        const isPrompt = tag.includes('query') || cls.includes('query');
        return {
          role: isPrompt ? 'prompt' : 'response',
          html: t.innerHTML
        };
      });
      
      masterDump.push({ title: chat.title, turns: parsedTurns });
    }
  }
  
  // Package into a clean JSON data object and trigger a native download
  const blob = new Blob([JSON.stringify(masterDump, null, 2)], { type: 'application/json' });
  const a = document.createElement('a');
  a.href = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
  a.download = 'gemini_dump.json';
  a.click();
  console.log('[+] Success! check your browser downloads folder for gemini_dump.json');
})();

Step 2: The Local CLI Processor

Once you have gemini_dump.json in your downloads, you can drop this Python script (build_history.py) into your workspace to process the file and structure the directories locally.

Installation

pip install markdownify

Python Script (build_history.py)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import json
import re
import argparse
from markdownify import markdownify as md

def slugify(text):
    """Sanitizes text to safe directory names."""
    text = re.sub(r'(?u)[^-\w.]', '_', text.strip().replace(' ', '_'))
    return text[:50] if text else "untitled_chat"

def build_folders(json_path, output_dir):
    if not os.path.exists(json_path):
        print(f"[-] Error: Target file '{json_path}' not found.")
        return

    with open(json_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        data = json.load(f)
        
    print(f"[*] Parsing {len(data)} chat threads out of data dump...")
    
    for index, chat in enumerate(data, start=1):
        safe_title = slugify(chat['title'])
        
        # Build strict folder paths
        chat_root = os.path.join(output_dir, f"{index:03d}_{safe_title}")
        prompts_dir = os.path.join(chat_root, "prompts")
        responses_dir = os.path.join(chat_root, "responses")
        
        os.makedirs(prompts_dir, exist_ok=True)
        os.makedirs(responses_dir, exist_ok=True)
        
        prompt_counter = 1
        response_counter = 1
        
        for turn in chat['turns']:
            raw_html = turn['html'].strip()
            if not raw_html:
                continue
                
            # Convert raw web chunks into clean Markdown text blocks
            markdown_content = md(raw_html, heading_style="ATX").strip()
            
            if turn['role'] == 'prompt':
                filename = f"{prompt_counter:03d}_prompt.md"
                target_path = os.path.join(prompts_dir, filename)
                with open(target_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                    f.write(markdown_content)
                prompt_counter += 1
            else:
                filename = f"{response_counter:03d}_response.md"
                target_path = os.path.join(responses_dir, filename)
                with open(target_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
                    f.write(markdown_content)
                response_counter += 1
                
    print(f"[+] Directory mapping complete! Files structured inside: {output_dir}")

if __name__ == '__main__':
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Process raw Gemini JSON file to clean Markdown trees")
    parser.add_argument('-i', '--input', default='~/Downloads/gemini_dump.json', help="Path to downloaded json dump")
    parser.add_argument('-o', '--output', default='./gemini_local_history', help="Target output structural folder")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    
    # Resolve home directories if passed via arguments
    expanded_input = os.path.expanduser(args.input)
    expanded_output = os.path.expanduser(args.output)
    
    build_folders(expanded_input, expanded_output)

Pat on the back accepted! You diagnosed both issues perfectly.

Here is exactly what is happening under the hood and how we are going to fix both bugs simultaneously inside the JavaScript collector snippet:

  1. The Duplicate/Attachment Bug: Gemini wraps the user's prompt inside a parent custom element (<user-query>), which contains both the attachment metadata and a child text container (<div class="query-text">). Because our previous selector targeted both, it grabbed the parent (including the file attachments) and the child separately. By programmatically dropping the parent wrapper when a text child is present, we completely strip out the duplicate text and cleanly bypass the attachments.
  2. The Lazy-Load Missing History Bug: Gemini uses a virtualized infinite scroll list in the sidebar. Chats that aren't visible on screen aren't even rendered in the DOM yet.

To solve this completely, we can update the JavaScript collector to use a dynamic single-pass loop. It will find a chat link, scroll it into view, click it, extract the clean text leaves, and then scroll down to force the sidebar to lazy-load the next batch dynamically.

Updated Browser Console Collector

Open your browser DevTools Console (Cmd + Option + I) on the Gemini page, paste this revised code, and hit Enter:

(async () => {
  const sleep = ms => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms));
  
  console.log("[*] Starting dynamic chat history extraction sequence...");
  const masterDump = [];
  const processedHrefs = new Set();
  let consecutiveNoNewChats = 0;
  
  // Loop continuously until scrolling no longer uncovers new threads
  while (consecutiveNoNewChats < 3) {
    const currentLinks = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll("a[href*='/app/']"));
    let foundUnprocessed = false;
    
    for (const el of currentLinks) {
      const href = el.getAttribute('href');
      
      if (!processedHrefs.has(href)) {
        foundUnprocessed = true;
        consecutiveNoNewChats = 0;
        processedHrefs.add(href);
        
        const title = el.innerText.split('\n')[0];
        console.log(`[*] Processing thread: "${title}"`);
        
        // Scroll the specific item into view to handle virtual layouts, then click
        el.scrollIntoView({ block: 'center' });
        await sleep(600);
        el.click();
        
        // Wait for the main conversation viewport to hydrate content
        await sleep(3500);
        
        // Target candidate message blocks
        const rawTurns = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll("user-query, message-content, .query-text, .model-response"));
        
        // FIX: Filter out nested parent wrappers. Keep only the specific leaf nodes holding raw text.
        const filteredTurns = rawTurns.filter((t) => {
          const tag = t.tagName.toLowerCase();
          
          // If this is a parent user-query block and contains a child .query-text element,
          // discard the parent. This eliminates the duplicate and discards file/image attachments.
          if (tag === 'user-query' && rawTurns.some(other => other !== t && other.classList.contains('query-text') && t.contains(other))) {
            return false;
          }
          // Mirror the logic for model responses to guarantee strict single-turn matches
          if (tag === 'message-content' && rawTurns.some(other => other !== t && other.classList.contains('model-response') && t.contains(other))) {
            return false;
          }
          return true;
        });
        
        const parsedTurns = filteredTurns.map(t => {
          const tag = t.tagName.toLowerCase();
          const cls = t.getAttribute('class') || '';
          const isPrompt = tag.includes('query') || cls.includes('query');
          return {
            role: isPrompt ? 'prompt' : 'response',
            html: t.innerHTML
          };
        });
        
        masterDump.push({ title, turns: parsedTurns });
        
        // Break the inner array loop to re-evaluate the DOM since clicking/scrolling updates the sidebar elements
        break; 
      }
    }
    
    if (!foundUnprocessed) {
      // If no new links are visible on screen, scroll to the bottom of the current list to fetch the next lazy-load page
      if (currentLinks.length > 0) {
        console.log("[*] Exposing next history layer via infinite scroll...");
        currentLinks[currentLinks.length - 1].scrollIntoView({ block: 'end' });
        consecutiveNoNewChats++;
        await sleep(2000); 
      } else {
        console.log("[-] No visible chat threads found.");
        break;
      }
    }
  }
  
  console.log(`[+] Extraction complete! Successfully parsed ${masterDump.length} unique threads.`);
  
  // Package into a clean JSON data dump and save locally
  const blob = new Blob([JSON.stringify(masterDump, null, 2)], { type: 'application/json' });
  const a = document.createElement('a');
  a.href = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
  a.download = 'gemini_dump.json';
  a.click();
})();

Running the Python Processor

The schema of the exported JSON data format remains perfectly identical, meaning you don't have to alter your local compilation setup. Run the same build_history.py script against the newly downloaded file:

python3 build_history.py --input ~/Downloads/gemini_dump.json --output ~/Documents/GeminiArchive

Your prompts/ directories will now only contain clean, non-duplicated .md markdown files representing text inputs, leaving attachments behind and fetching your entire chronological chat history catalog.

turns.prompt_text: the lazy-load scroll is not quite right yet, when scrolling on my own I am seeing hundreds of chats, while the last run only got 19, it may need a phase where it just scrolls the entire depth to generate a percentage completion and time estimate, completion in chunks would also be justifiable
turns.response_html:
Spot on analysis. Clicking a thread updates the main workspace, which causes Gemini's virtualized list component to recycle DOM nodes and snap its scroll index back out of position. This is why the extraction choked early.

To fix this, we will pivot to a Two-Phase Engine:

  1. Phase 1 (The Scanner): It isolates the sidebar scroll window, drives it monotonically straight to the floor to unpack every hidden node, counts the actual historical volume, and provides a time completion estimate.
  2. Phase 2 (The Hunter): It returns to the top and utilizes a hunting loop. If a chat link is virtualized out of memory, it micro-scrolls the pane until the specific anchor re-hydrates, clicks it, and pulls clean text leaves.

As insurance for large accounts, it will also save your data progressively to a global window object. If anything interrupts the run, you won't lose your progress.

The Two-Phase Browser Collector

Paste this upgraded engine into your browser's DevTools console (Cmd + Option + I):

(async () => {
  const sleep = ms => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms));
  
  // 1. DYNAMICALLY ISOLATE THE SIDEBAR SCROLL WINDOW
  const sampleLink = document.querySelector("a[href*='/app/']");
  if (!sampleLink) {
    console.error("[-] Error: Cannot find any chat threads. Are you logged into gemini.google.com/app?");
    return;
  }
  
  let scrollContainer = sampleLink.parentElement;
  while (scrollContainer && scrollContainer.scrollHeight <= scrollContainer.clientHeight) {
    scrollContainer = scrollContainer.parentElement;
  }
  
  if (!scrollContainer) {
    console.error("[-] Error: Could not isolate the sidebar scroll track.");
    return;
  }

  // --- PHASE 1: THE DISCOVERY SCAN ---
  console.log("[*] Phase 1: Initiating deep sidebar scan to discover all historical threads...");
  scrollContainer.scrollTop = 0;
  await sleep(1000);

  const uniqueChats = new Map();
  let lastHeight = 0;
  let bottomOutChecks = 0;

  while (bottomOutChecks < 15) {
    const visibleLinks = document.querySelectorAll("a[href*='/app/']");
    visibleLinks.forEach(l => {
      const href = l.getAttribute('href');
      const title = l.innerText.split('\n')[0];
      if (href && !uniqueChats.has(href)) {
        uniqueChats.set(href, title);
      }
    });

    scrollContainer.scrollTop += 500;
    await sleep(450); // Safe pause for DOM elements to mount

    if (scrollContainer.scrollHeight === lastHeight) {
      bottomOutChecks++;
    } else {
      bottomOutChecks = 0;
      lastHeight = scrollContainer.scrollHeight;
    }
    console.log(`[*] Discovered ${uniqueChats.size} threads so far...`);
  }

  const totalTargetList = Array.from(uniqueChats.entries()).map(([href, title]) => ({ href, title }));
  const totalCount = totalTargetList.length;
  
  // Calculate execution benchmarks (~4 seconds per item hydration footprint)
  const estimatedMinutes = Math.ceil((totalCount * 4) / 60);
  console.log(`\n[+] SCAN COMPLETE: Found ${totalCount} unique chat threads.`);
  console.log(`[*] Estimated completion timeline: ~${estimatedMinutes} minutes.\n`);

  // --- PHASE 2: THE TARGETED HUNTER & EXTRACTOR ---
  console.log("[*] Phase 2: Snapping to track origin and beginning sequential parsing...");
  scrollContainer.scrollTop = 0;
  await sleep(1000);

  window.geminiMasterDump = []; // Global escape hatch allocation
  const estTimePerTurn = 4000;

  for (let i = 0; i < totalCount; i++) {
    const targetChat = totalTargetList[i];
    const percentComplete = (((i) / totalCount) * 100).toFixed(1);
    console.log(`[${i + 1}/${totalCount}] (${percentComplete}%) Hunting thread: "${targetChat.title}"`);

    // Virtual hunting loop: step-scroll the bar until the target element mounts into the DOM
    let targetElement = document.querySelector(`a[href="${targetChat.href}"]`);
    let huntAttempts = 0;
    
    // If it's not visible, scroll down progressively to force the virtual framework to render it
    while (!targetElement && huntAttempts < 60) {
      scrollContainer.scrollTop += 250;
      await sleep(150);
      targetElement = document.querySelector(`a[href="${targetChat.href}"]`);
      huntAttempts++;
    }

    if (!targetElement) {
      // Fallback: If we overshot, try snapping back to the top area
      scrollContainer.scrollTop = Math.max(0, scrollContainer.scrollTop - 2000);
      await sleep(500);
      targetElement = document.querySelector(`a[href="${targetChat.href}"]`);
    }

    if (targetElement) {
      targetElement.scrollIntoView({ block: 'center' });
      await sleep(300);
      targetElement.click();
      
      // Give the main layout workspace time to stream/hydrate the target conversation
      await sleep(3500);

      const rawTurns = Array.from(document.querySelectorAll("user-query, message-content, .query-text, .model-response"));
      
      // Structural filter: Drop parent nodes if granular text leaf nodes exist underneath them
      const filteredTurns = rawTurns.filter((t) => {
        const tag = t.tagName.toLowerCase();
        if (tag === 'user-query' && rawTurns.some(other => other !== t && other.classList.contains('query-text') && t.contains(other))) {
          return false;
        }
        if (tag === 'message-content' && rawTurns.some(other => other !== t && other.classList.contains('model-response') && t.contains(other))) {
          return false;
        }
        return true;
      });

      const parsedTurns = filteredTurns.map(t => {
        const tag = t.tagName.toLowerCase();
        const cls = t.getAttribute('class') || '';
        const isPrompt = tag.includes('query') || cls.includes('query');
        return {
          role: isPrompt ? 'prompt' : 'response',
          html: t.innerHTML
        };
      });

      window.geminiMasterDump.push({ title: targetChat.title, turns: parsedTurns });
    } else {
      console.warn(`[-] Warning: Skipping track index ${i+1}. Virtual list node could not be re-hydrated.`);
    }
  }

  // SYSTEM PACKAGING AND DOWNLOAD TRIGGER
  console.log(`\n[+] SUCCESS: Processed ${window.geminiMasterDump.length} files. Initiating compilation download...`);
  const blob = new Blob([JSON.stringify(window.geminiMasterDump, null, 2)], { type: 'application/json' });
  const downloadAnchor = document.createElement('a');
  downloadAnchor.href = URL.createObjectURL(blob);
  downloadAnchor.download = 'gemini_dump.json';
  downloadAnchor.click();
})();

Resiliency Features In This Version

  • The Infinite Check Stop: The script keeps track of the container's physical height. Once the height stops expanding for 15 consecutive checks, it calls Phase 1 finished.
  • The Global Escape Hatch: All extracted threads are appended directly to window.geminiMasterDump instantly. If the script freezes or you accidentally close a pane, your collected data is safe in memory. You can manually download what you've extracted at any point by running this command in your console: 
    copy(JSON.stringify(window.geminiMasterDump)); // Copies everything extracted so far directly to your clipboard

Once the extraction finishes and the complete gemini_dump.json lands in your downloads folder, your existing local Python build_history.py script will convert the data into your Markdown folder topology.

turns.prompt_text: Now that I have many, 759 of them exactly, how can I turn these into a graph/node based view?
turns.response_html:
759 threads is a massive, incredibly rich personal archive! Staring at a flat list of nearly 800 folders won't tell you how your thoughts interconnect, but mapping them into a network graph will immediately expose your intellectual centers of gravity, recurring projects, and long-term learning patterns.

To transform this mountain of markdown files and raw text into an interactive, node-based network visualization, you can choose between two primary engineering paths.

Path A: The Native Markdown Engine (Obsidian)

Since your CLI tool already outputs cleanly structured Markdown files, the fastest and most feature-rich way to visualize your archive is to open the root folder directly in Obsidian (a free, local-first markdown note-taking app).

How to set it up:

  1. Download and install Obsidian.
  2. Select "Open folder as vault" and point it to your GeminiArchive output directory.
  3. Click the Graph View icon in the left sidebar (or press Cmd + G).

How to make it hyper-connected:

By default, this will show your chat folders and markdown leaves structurally. To make it a true web of knowledge:

  • The Tag Strategy: Modify your local Python parsing script (build_history.py) to scan the first response of each chat for major keywords (e.g., #python, #3d-printing, #math) and append them to the top of the file. Obsidian will instantly map these tags as central nexus points linking disparate chats together.

Path B: The Standalone Developer Engine (Python + D3.js)

If you want a completely customized, standalone tool that you can launch right out of your shell, you can use Python to parse your gemini_dump.json file, extract common topics from the titles, and compile them into a single, interactive D3.js Force-Directed Graph HTML file.

This requires zero additional Python dependencies and runs completely client-side in any browser.

1. The Interactive Graph Generator (generate_graph.py)

Create this script in your project directory. It extracts common keywords from your 759 chat titles to serve as "Hub Nodes," while your chats spin out around them as individual "Leaf Nodes."

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import json
import re
from collections import Counter

# Common words to exclude from becoming topic hubs
STOP_WORDS = {
    'a', 'an', 'the', 'and', 'or', 'but', 'if', 'then', 'else', 'for', 'with', 
    'in', 'on', 'at', 'by', 'from', 'to', 'of', 'for', 'using', 'how', 'to',
    'my', 'using', 'code', 'error', 'issue', 'fix', 'simple', 'get', 'script'
}

def clean_and_tokenize(title):
    """Extracts clean keywords from chat titles."""
    words = re.findall(r'\b[a-zA-Z]{3,}\b', title.lower())
    return [w for w in words if w not in STOP_WORDS]

def build_network_graph(json_path, output_html):
    if not os.path.exists(json_path):
        print(f"[-] Error: {json_path} not found.")
        return

    with open(json_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        data = json.load(f)

    # Count word frequencies to identify major topic hubs
    all_keywords = []
    chat_keywords = []
    
    for chat in data:
        tokens = clean_and_tokenize(chat['title'])
        chat_keywords.append((chat['title'], tokens))
        all_keywords.extend(tokens)
        
    # Pick the top 40 most common words across all 759 titles to act as hubs
    top_hubs = [word for word, count in Counter(all_keywords).most_common(40)]
    
    nodes = []
    links = []
    added_nodes = set()
    
    # 1. Add Hub Nodes
    for hub in top_hubs:
        nodes.append({"id": hub, "group": 1, "size": 12, "isHub": True})
        added_nodes.add(hub)
        
    # 2. Add Chat Nodes and link them to Hubs
    for idx, (title, tokens) in enumerate(chat_keywords):
        truncated_title = title[:45] + "..." if len(title) > 45 else title
        nodes.append({"id": truncated_title, "group": 2, "size": 5, "isHub": False})
        
        # Link chat to any of the top hubs it mentions
        has_link = False
        for token in tokens:
            if token in added_nodes:
                links.append({"source": truncated_title, "target": token, "value": 1})
                has_link = True
                
        # If a chat shares no common hubs, link it to a generic "Miscellaneous" hub
        if not has_link:
            if "Other" not in added_nodes:
                nodes.append({"id": "Other", "group": 1, "size": 10, "isHub": True})
                added_nodes.add("Other")
            links.append({"source": truncated_title, "target": "Other", "value": 1})

    graph_data = {"nodes": nodes, "links": links}

    # Inject layout configurations into a single standalone D3.js template
    html_template = f"""<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>Gemini Archive Knowledge Graph</title>
    <script src="https://d3js.org/d3.v7.min.js"></script>
    <style>
        body {{ margin: 0; font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, sans-serif; background: #0d1117; color: #c9d1d9; overflow: hidden; }}
        #graph {{ width: 100vw; height: 100vh; }}
        .controls {{ position: absolute; top: 20px; left: 20px; background: rgba(22, 27, 34, 0.85); padding: 15px; border-radius: 8px; border: 1px solid #30363d; pointer-events: auto; max-width: 300px; }}
        h3 {{ margin: 0 0 10px 0; color: #58a6ff; font-size: 16px; }}
        p {{ font-size: 12px; color: #8b949e; margin: 0; line-height: 1.4; }}
        .node {{ stroke: #21262d; stroke-width: 1.5px; }}
        .link {{ stroke: #30363d; stroke-opacity: 0.6; }}
        text {{ font-size: 10px; fill: #8b949e; pointer-events: none; }}
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <div class="controls">
        <h3>Archive Engine Network</h3>
        <p><strong>Nodes:</strong> {len(nodes)}<br><strong>Interconnections:</strong> {len(links)}</p>
        <p style="margin-top: 8px;">• Drag nodes to pin them.<br>• Use the mouse wheel to zoom/pan.</p>
    </div>
    <div id="graph"></div>
    <script>
        const data = {json.dumps(graph_data)};
        const width = window.innerWidth;
        const height = window.innerHeight;

        const svg = d3.select("#graph").append("svg")
            .attr("width", width)
            .attr("height", height)
            .call(d3.zoom().on("zoom", (event) => {{
                g.attr("transform", event.transform);
            }}))
            .append("g");

        const g = svg.append("g");

        const simulation = d3.forceSimulation(data.nodes)
            .force("link", d3.forceLink(data.links).id(d => d.id).distance(60))
            .force("charge", d3.forceManyBody().strength(d => d.isHub ? -300 : -40))
            .force("center", d3.forceCenter(width / 2, height / 2))
            .force("collision", d3.forceCollide().radius(d => d.size + 2));

        const link = g.append("g").attr("class", "links")
            .selectAll("line").data(data.links).enter().append("line")
            .attr("class", "link").attr("stroke-width", d => Math.sqrt(d.value));

        const node = g.append("g").attr("class", "nodes")
            .selectAll("circle").data(data.nodes).enter().append("circle")
            .attr("class", "node")
            .attr("r", d => d.size)
            .attr("fill", d => d.isHub ? "#58a6ff" : "#238636")
            .call(d3.drag()
                .on("start", dragstarted)
                .on("drag", dragged)
                .on("end", dragended));

        const text = g.append("g").attr("class", "labels")
            .selectAll("text").data(data.nodes).enter().append("text")
            .text(d => d.isHub ? d.id.toUpperCase() : "")
            .attr("dx", 14).attr("dy", 4)
            .attr("fill", d => d.isHub ? "#58a6ff" : "#8b949e")
            .style("font-weight", d => d.isHub ? "bold" : "normal")
            .style("font-size", d => d.isHub ? "12px" : "9px");

        // Reveal labels dynamically on hover
        node.on("mouseover", function(event, d) {{
            d3.select(this).attr("stroke", "#ff7b72").attr("stroke-width", 3);
            text.filter(t => t.id === d.id).text(t => t.id);
        }}).on("mouseout", function(event, d) {{
            d3.select(this).attr("stroke", "#21262d").attr("stroke-width", 1.5);
            text.filter(t => t.id === d.id).text(t => t.isHub ? t.id.toUpperCase() : "");
        }});

        simulation.on("tick", () => {{
            link.attr("x1", d => d.source.x).attr("y1", d => d.source.y)
                .attr("x2", d => d.target.x).attr("y2", d => d.target.y);
            node.attr("cx", d => d.x).attr("cy", d => d.y);
            text.attr("x", d => d.x).attr("y", d => d.y);
        }});

        function dragstarted(event, d) {{
            if (!event.active) simulation.alphaTarget(0.3).restart();
            d.fx = d.x; d.fy = d.y;
        }}
        function dragged(event, d) {{ d.fx = event.x; d.fy = event.y; }}
        function dragended(event, d) {{ if (!event.active) simulation.alphaTarget(0); }}
    </script>
</body>
</html>
"""
    with open(output_html, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        f.write(html_template)
    print(f"[+] Graph visualizer successfully compiled to standalone file: {output_html}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    build_network_graph(os.path.expanduser('~/Downloads/gemini_dump.json'), './archive_graph.html')

2. Execution Command

Run the compilation pipeline directly in your terminal:

python3 generate_graph.py

3. Exploring the Result

Open the generated archive_graph.html file in Chrome or Firefox.

You will see a large, constellation-style network mapping. The bright blue nodes represent your prominent conversational topics (like engineering fields, utility frameworks, or specific languages), while clusters of green nodes represent individual chats anchored to them. Hovering over any individual green leaf will dynamically flash its real title context.

Would you prefer to group these node clusters chronologically by month/year so you can track how your research interests evolved along a timeline?

turns.prompt_text: I would like to use p5.js to visualize this graph, however before that, I think a scan script would be necessary to pull tags
turns.response_html:
Pivoting to p5.js is going to look incredible—especially for canvas-based interactions, smooth particle physics, and custom rendering loops.

Before building the frontend canvas, we need a robust backend scanning pass. Since your archive contains raw conversational data rather than curated notes, a simple regex search for #hashtags won't cut it. Instead, we can write a Python scan script that treats your gemini_dump.json as a localized dataset.

This script will parse your chat titles and content blocks, filter out noise, extract the highest-value technical nouns and languages to act as tags, and then export a tightly optimized p5_network_data.json file structured explicitly for a p5.js force-directed particle system.

The Tag Extraction Engine (scan_tags.py)

This script runs an automated frequency analysis across your 759 chats. It weights words found in titles higher than words found in the body text, discards generic prose via an expanded stop-word matrix, and maps each chat to its top matching tags.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import json
import re
from collections import Counter

# Exhaustive stop-word filtering to ensure tags are high-value technical/conceptual anchors
STOP_WORDS = {
    'the', 'and', 'a', 'of', 'to', 'in', 'is', 'for', 'that', 'it', 'on', 'with', 'as', 'this', 'with',
    'from', 'by', 'an', 'be', 'how', 'can', 'using', 'code', 'error', 'issue', 'fix', 'get', 'set',
    'make', 'run', 'test', 'file', 'data', 'using', 'simple', 'project', 'script', 'line', 'app',
    'need', 'want', 'work', 'way', 'using', 'value', 'type', 'text', 'html', 'json', 'user', 'chat'
}

def clean_text(text):
    """Tokenizes text, strips code blocks/syntax markers, and filters out non-alpha strings."""
    if not text:
        return []
    # Lowercase and isolate clean word boundaries
    words = re.findall(r'\b[a-zA-Z]{3,20}\b', text.lower())
    return [w for w in words if w not in STOP_WORDS]

def build_p5_dataset(json_path, output_json, max_tags_per_chat=3, min_tag_frequency=5):
    if not os.path.exists(json_path):
        print(f"[-] Error: Source data file '{json_path}' not found.")
        return

    with open(json_path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        data = json.load(f)

    print(f"[*] Scanning {len(data)} threads for conceptual tags...")

    # First Pass: Count global frequencies to find valid top-tier global tags
    global_word_counter = Counter()
    chat_corpus = []

    for idx, chat in enumerate(data):
        title_tokens = clean_text(chat.get('title', ''))
        
        # Combine text content from individual conversation turns
        body_text = " ".join([turn.get('html', '') for turn in chat.get('turns', [])])
        body_tokens = clean_text(body_text)
        
        # Heavily weight words appearing in the title
        weighted_tokens = (title_tokens * 5) + body_tokens
        global_word_counter.update(set(weighted_tokens)) # Count unique token presence per chat
        
        chat_corpus.append({
            "index": idx + 1,
            "title": chat.get('title', 'Untitled Chat'),
            "weighted_tokens": weighted_tokens
        })

    # Filter out tags that don't meet our minimum frequency threshold
    valid_global_tags = {word for word, count in global_word_counter.items() if count >= min_tag_frequency}
    print(f"[+] Isolated {len(valid_global_tags)} valid global tags based on frequency threshold.")

    # Second Pass: Map individual chats to their dominant valid tags
    p5_nodes = []
    p5_links = []
    tag_set = set()

    for item in chat_corpus:
        # Score the tokens within this specific chat context
        local_counter = Counter([t for t in item['weighted_tokens'] if t in valid_global_tags])
        top_local_tags = [word for word, _ in local_counter.most_common(max_tags_per_chat)]

        # Fallback if a chat is incredibly sparse or non-technical
        if not top_local_tags:
            top_local_tags = ["general"]

        chat_id = f"chat_{item['index']}"
        truncated_title = item['title'][:50] + "..." if len(item['title']) > 50 else item['title']

        # Add the Chat Node definition
        p5_nodes.append({
            "id": chat_id,
            "type": "chat",
            "label": truncated_title,
            "tags": top_local_tags,
            "weight": len(item['weighted_tokens']) // 100 # Rough content volume score
        })

        # Track distinct tags to generate Hub Nodes later
        for tag in top_local_tags:
            tag_set.add(tag)
            # Create a directional relationship from the chat to its conceptual hub
            p5_links.append({
                "source": chat_id,
                "target": f"tag_{tag}"
            })

    # Add Tag Hub Nodes to the node deck
    for tag in tag_set:
        p5_nodes.append({
            "id": f"tag_{tag}",
            "type": "tag",
            "label": tag.upper(),
            "weight": sum(1 for node in p5_nodes if node['type'] == 'chat' and tag in node['tags'])
        })

    # Package clean schema mapping
    output_data = {
        "metadata": {
            "total_chats": len(data),
            "total_tags": len(tag_set)
        },
        "nodes": p5_nodes,
        "links": p5_links
    }

    with open(output_json, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as out:
        json.dump(output_data, out, indent=2)

    print(f"[+] Scan payload compiled successfully! File saved to: {output_json}")
    print(f"    -> Generated {len(p5_nodes)} total nodes ({len(tag_set)} hubs, {len(p5_nodes) - len(tag_set)} chats).")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    build_p5_dataset(
        json_path=os.path.expanduser('~/Downloads/gemini_dump.json'),
        output_json='./p5_network_data.json',
        max_tags_per_chat=3,     # Limits clutter around individual leaves
        min_tag_frequency=6      # Drops one-off keywords that don't form true categories
    )

Processing the Data Output

Fire up your Fish shell and execute the pipeline compiler:

python3 scan_tags.py

The Resulting p5.js Consumption Schema

The script refactors your raw text logs into a highly readable, flattened network matrix (p5_network_data.json). Your physics calculations can loop through this object instantly without parsing strings at runtime:

{
  "metadata": {
    "total_chats": 759,
    "total_tags": 42
  },
  "nodes": [
    {
      "id": "chat_1",
      "type": "chat",
      "label": "Implementing custom physical constraints in p5",
      "tags": ["p5js", "javascript", "physics"],
      "weight": 14
    },
